title: What is React?
summary: **React** is a declarative, component-based JavaScript library for building user interfaces. You describe what the UI should look like for a given state, and React efficiently updates the DOM to match.

subtopics.title: Declarative UI
subtopics.explanation: You say what the screen should show, and React works out how to update it. It is like telling a map your destination instead of giving every turn yourself.

subtopics.title: Components
subtopics.explanation: A component is a reusable piece of a page, such as a button or menu. It is like a building block: combine small blocks to make a larger page.

subtopics.title: Virtual DOM
subtopics.explanation: The virtual DOM is React's in-memory description of the page. React compares the old and new descriptions before changing the browser page, like checking two drafts and marking only the changed lines.

subtopics.title: One-way data flow
subtopics.explanation: Data usually moves from a parent component down to its children. This makes it easier to find where a value came from, like following a package from sender to recipient.

subtopics.title: Reconciliation
subtopics.explanation: Reconciliation is how React decides which visible parts need updating. It compares the previous screen description with the new one, much like spotting differences between two photos.

subtopics.title: Library vs framework
subtopics.explanation: React focuses on building the visible part of an app. Other tools can add routing or data loading, like choosing extra tools for a toolbox instead of buying one fixed kit.

foundations.overview: React helps you build a webpage from reusable pieces. You describe what each piece should show, and React updates the page when its data changes. Think of it like a digital noticeboard: change the message, and React refreshes the right part.
foundations.formalDefinition: React is an open-source JavaScript library, created and maintained by Meta, for building composable user interfaces using a declarative programming model. Components return a description of the UI (typically written in JSX); React reconciles that description against the current UI and applies the necessary updates to the host environment (the DOM in browsers).
foundations.whyItMatters: React reframed UI development around state. Rather than imperatively mutating the DOM as events happen, you keep state in one place and let React derive the UI from it. This eliminates a whole class of bugs where the screen and the data drift out of sync, and it scales from a single widget to applications with thousands of components.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of your UI as a pure function: UI = f(state). When the state changes, you re-run the function to get a new description of the UI, and React works out the difference between the old and new descriptions, touching only the parts of the DOM that actually changed.
foundations.browserPerspective: In the browser, React keeps a lightweight in-memory representation of the UI (the Virtual DOM / fiber tree). When state changes, React builds a new tree, diffs it against the previous one (reconciliation), and then makes the smallest possible set of real DOM mutations. The browser only repaints the nodes that genuinely changed, which is far cheaper than rebuilding everything.
foundations.realWorldUsage: React powers Facebook, Instagram, Netflix's UI, Airbnb, and countless dashboards, e-commerce sites, and internal tools. It is also the foundation for meta-frameworks like Next.js and Remix, and for React Native, which renders to native mobile views instead of the DOM.
foundations.businessImpact: React's component model lets teams ship features faster by reusing UI pieces and reasoning about each component in isolation. Its huge ecosystem and talent pool reduce hiring and onboarding costs, which is why it is the default choice for many product teams.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Declarative, component-based code is easier to test, reason about, and refactor than imperative DOM manipulation. One-way data flow makes data movement predictable, so engineers can trace where a value comes from and what re-renders when it changes.
foundations.performanceImpact: React's diffing avoids unnecessary DOM work, but the Virtual DOM is not free — re-rendering large trees or doing heavy work in render can cause jank. Understanding when components re-render is key to keeping React apps fast.
commonUseCases: Single-page applications (SPAs) with rich, stateful UIs
Reusable design-system components shared across a product
Dashboards and admin panels that update as data changes
Server-rendered apps via meta-frameworks like Next.js

commonMisconceptions.myth: React is a full framework like Angular.
commonMisconceptions.reality: React is a focused UI library. Routing, data fetching, and state management are handled by separate libraries you choose, which is why React is often paired with tools like React Router or Next.js.

commonMisconceptions.myth: The Virtual DOM makes React faster than plain DOM manipulation.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Hand-tuned vanilla JS can be faster in micro-benchmarks. The Virtual DOM's value is predictable, maintainable updates at scale — not raw speed.

visualExplorer.title: The component tree
visualExplorer.caption: A React app is a tree of components. Data flows down through props from parent to child — explore how the pieces nest together.

interactiveExamples.title: Declarative UI from state
interactiveExamples.explanation: Notice you never touch the DOM directly. You hold a value in state and describe what the UI should look like for that value; React updates the screen when the value changes.
interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: A heading and a button. Clicking the button toggles both the heading text and the button label.

interactiveExamples.title: Composing components
interactiveExamples.explanation: A React UI is built from components that nest inside one another, just like HTML elements. Here App renders two Greeting components, each customised with a prop.
interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: A heading followed by two greeting lines, one for Ada and one for Linus.

codeLab.title: Render a value declaratively
codeLab.instructions: Create a component that holds a name in state and renders 'Welcome, <name>' in an <h2>. Add a button that changes the name to 'World' when clicked. Do not touch the DOM directly — let React render from state.
codeLab.expectedOutput: A heading that reads 'Welcome, World' after the button is clicked.
hints: Hold the name in useState so React re-renders when it changes.
Read the state value inside the JSX with {name} instead of writing to the DOM.

keyTakeaways: React is a declarative, component-based library for building user interfaces.
You describe the UI as a function of state (UI = f(state)); React updates the DOM to match.
Components compose into a tree, and data flows one way — down via props.
The Virtual DOM and reconciliation let React apply minimal, efficient DOM updates.
React is a focused UI library, not a full framework — you choose tools for routing and data.
